claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between diffusion-controlled Al ordering and thermodynamic instability of the BCC state.
Suppression of Al diffusion during rapid cooling kinetically retains the BCC phase.
Intermediate-temperature exposure permits Al diffusion and initiates long-range ordering that transforms the phase.
The proposed structural mediator is an Al-rich, long-range-ordered phase produced by Al segregation and ordering.
The ordered phase may have B2, L12, or another structure.
The BCC phase is thermodynamically stable at high temperature but metastable after cooling.
Intermediate-temperature holding enhances Al mobility and triggers local compositional fluctuations and ordering.
Al ordering locally lowers free energy and drives transformation to an ordered phase.
A rapid quench prevents diffusion-mediated kinetic ordering.
Aging between approximately 500°C and 700°C will produce additional or split diffraction peaks associated with an ordered phase.
The rapidly quenched baseline will retain a homogeneous, metastable BCC diffraction signature without long-range ordering.
The proposed ordering mechanism is active primarily between roughly 500°C and 700°C.
At very low temperatures, frozen diffusion masks the ordering transformation.
At very high temperatures, homogenization or dissolution of ordering tendencies masks the ordering transformation.
The exact transformation kinetics and identity of the ordered phase are uncertain and may depend on interactions among the other alloying elements.
Failure to detect any diffraction, microscopy, or thermal-signature change after extended intermediate-temperature aging would falsify the proposed Al-diffusion-mediated ordering mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the high-temperature BCC state intrinsically thermodynamically unstable, whereas the mechanism states that BCC is stable at high temperature and becomes metastable only upon cooling. The temperature at which the claimed instability applies is therefore inconsistent or ambiguous.
